title: Trapping Rain Water — two-pointer tracking left-max and right-max.
shortTitle: Trapping Rain Water — Two-Pointer Left-Max and Right-Max

s1_definition.profdef: Trapping Rain Water takes an array of bar heights and computes how much water would be trapped between the bars after rain. The water held above any single bar equals the smaller of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right, minus that bar's own height, never less than zero. The optimal solution uses two pointers from both ends while tracking a running left maximum and right maximum, adding trapped water at the shorter side each step. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.

Water over any day is limited by the shorter of the highest day to its left and the highest day to its right. Two fingers walk inward from both ends, each remembering the tallest wall seen so far on its side, and whichever side is shorter is the side whose trapped water we can safely add.

s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Trapping Rain Water takes an array of bar heights and computes how much water would be trapped between the bars after rain. The water held above any single bar equals the smaller of the tallest bar to its left and the tallest bar to its right, minus that bar's own height, never less than zero. The optimal solution uses two pointers from both ends while tracking a running left maximum and right maximum, adding trapped water at the shorter side each step. It runs in linear time with constant extra space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India plots Rajesh's daily balances as a skyline of bars, and an analyst wants to know how much "reserve" sits trapped in the dips between tall balance days. Water over any day is limited by the shorter of the highest day to its left and the highest day to its right. Two fingers walk inward from both ends, each remembering the tallest wall seen so far on its side, and whichever side is shorter is the side whose trapped water we can safely add.

**One line to remember:** Water over a bar is min(leftMax, rightMax) minus the bar height, and two pointers add it from the shorter side.

sections.s2_technical:
The brute force asks, for each bar, what is the tallest bar to its left and the tallest to its right, then adds the smaller of those two minus the current height. Done naively that is quadratic because each bar scans both directions. A precompute version stores leftMax and rightMax arrays in two passes and then sums in a third pass, which is linear time but uses extra arrays.

The two-pointer method gets linear time with only constant space. You put a left pointer at the first bar and a right pointer at the last bar, and you keep two running values, leftMax and rightMax, both starting at zero. At each step you look at which side is shorter. If the bar at the left pointer is less than or equal to the bar at the right pointer, you process the left side: if the current left bar is taller than leftMax you update leftMax, otherwise you add leftMax minus the current bar to the trapped total, then move left inward. Symmetrically, if the right bar is smaller you process the right side with rightMax and move right inward.

The reason this is correct is the key insight. When the left bar is less than or equal to the right bar, you know the right side has at least one wall as tall as the right bar, which is at least as tall as the left bar. So the water over the left bar is limited by leftMax alone, because the right side can guarantee a wall that is tall enough and the true limit is the smaller side. That guarantee is what lets you commit the left side's water immediately without knowing the exact rightMax yet.

A senior point is proving the invariant. At every moment, everything to the left of the left pointer has been fully accounted for, everything to the right of the right pointer has been fully accounted for, and leftMax and rightMax are the true maxima of the processed-and-current regions on each side. Because you only commit water on the side whose boundary is guaranteed smaller, you never over-count or under-count.

Another senior point is overflow and money precision. If the heights are amounts I use BigDecimal and compute the trapped water with subtract and compareTo, adding with add, so totals are exact. I also guard the empty or single-bar case by returning zero, since no water can be trapped without at least three bars forming a dip.

A small finance-domain example: `int l=0,r=n-1; BigDecimal lMax=ZERO,rMax=ZERO,water=ZERO; while(l<r){ if(h[l].compareTo(h[r])<=0){ if(h[l].compareTo(lMax)>=0) lMax=h[l]; else water=water.add(lMax.subtract(h[l])); l++; } else { ... r-- } }` accumulates the trapped reserve exactly.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India draws Rajesh's daily closing balances as a bar skyline, and a liquidity-analytics feature measures the "trapped reserve", the total water that would collect in the dips between his higher balance days, as an intuitive picture of idle funds sitting between peaks. The feature must run fast even over years of daily data. Computing trapped rain water with two pointers is exactly this.

This is exactly how Trapping Rain Water works in Java — two pointers walk inward while tracking the tallest wall on each side and adding water on the shorter side.

Problem 2 — Balances are exact BigDecimal amounts, so the trapped water and the running maxima must be computed precisely, and the feature must return zero when there are fewer than three days since no dip can hold water. This shows money data-type care and the degenerate-case guard.

What the code will do: a `RainWaterAnalyzer` with `trappedReserve(BigDecimal[] heights)` using the two-pointer left-max and right-max technique, accumulating the trapped water in BigDecimal. The demo computes the trapped reserve for Rajesh's daily balances.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: the balance skyline is `0, 1, 0, 2, 1, 0, 1, 3, 2, 1, 2, 1`.

Step 1: left starts at index zero with height `0`, right at the last index with height `1`, leftMax and rightMax both zero, water zero. Because the left height `0` is less than or equal to the right height `1`, we process the left side. The left bar `0` is not below leftMax, so leftMax becomes `0`, and we move left to index one.

Step 2: left bar is `1`, right bar is `1`. Left is less than or equal to right, so we process left. The bar `1` is above leftMax `0`, so leftMax becomes `1`, no water added, and left moves to index two.

Step 3: left bar is `0`, right bar is `1`. We process the left side. The bar `0` is below leftMax `1`, so we add leftMax minus bar, which is `1 - 0 = 1`, making water `1`, then move left to index three.

Step 4: as the pointers continue inward, each dip below the tracked maximum contributes trapped water. Over the full run the dips at indices two, four, five, six, and nine contribute water totaling six units, because at every step we commit water only on the side whose boundary is guaranteed smaller.

Step 5: eventually the left and right pointers meet, the loop ends, and water holds the final total of `6`. The scan touched every bar exactly once with only a handful of running values, so it used constant extra space.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26T18:20:00Z INFO Trapped reserve = 6
2026-10-26T18:20:00Z INFO Trapped reserve for Rajesh = 6
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [0,1,0,2,1,0,1,3,2,1,2,1]  l=0 r=11 leftMax=0 rightMax=0 water=0
    │
    ▼
  while l<r: process the SHORTER side; add (sideMax - bar) if bar is lower
    │ l:0 → leftMax=0            l++
    │ l:1 → leftMax=1            l++
    │ l:0 → water += 1 (=1)      l++
    │ ... dips keep adding → water = 6
    ▼
  water = 6 (trapped reserve)
    ▼
  Output: idle funds trapped between balance peaks
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Trapping Rain Water takes an array of bar heights and computes the total water trapped in the dips after rain, where the water over any bar equals the smaller of the tallest wall to its left and the tallest wall to its right, minus that bar's own height. I solve it with two pointers from both ends while tracking a running left maximum and right maximum, committing trapped water on whichever side is currently shorter. It is a single linear pass with constant extra space, better than the quadratic brute force and tighter than the precompute version that needs two extra arrays.

The insight interviewers want is why committing on the shorter side is safe. When the left bar is less than or equal to the right bar, the right side already guarantees a wall at least as tall, so the water over the left bar is bounded purely by the left maximum, and I can add it immediately without knowing the exact right maximum yet. That guarantee, maintained as an invariant on both sides, is what makes the single pass correct rather than lucky.

I also handle precision and edge cases. For money I use BigDecimal with subtract, add, and compareTo so totals are exact, and I return zero when there are fewer than three bars since no dip can hold water. These guards matter in a banking system where silent rounding or an off-by-one on a tiny input would corrupt a reported figure.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to power a liquidity-reserve analytic, drawing Rajesh's daily balances as a skyline and measuring the idle funds that collect in the dips between his higher balance days, computed quickly even over years of data. Explaining the commit-the-shorter-side rule and the running-maximum invariant shows the interviewer that I understand this classic two-pointer problem deeply, which is exactly the depth it is designed to test.

keyPoints: Two pointers from opposite ends: pair sum, container with most water
Two pointers same direction: remove duplicates, merge sorted arrays
Three pointers: 3Sum — sort + fix one + two-pointer scan
Fast/slow: linked list cycle, middle element
